Maladaptive Strategies.value: I eat more than usual to distract myself or feel better
I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied

Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Negative Appraisals.value: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.item: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study' appears internally inconsistent as written: it names avoidance but the item content states engagement in work/study rather than avoidance. That is a within-item contradiction in the Maladaptive Strategies node.

issues.item: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
issues.explanation: For trauma type of life-threatening illness, prominent movement-triggered hypervigilant startle responses are not impossible, but paired with the rest of the profile they suggest an external immediate-danger trauma context more than illness-related threat. Because the formulation has no active Triggers links and no Memory involvement, these threat items lack a coherent illness-specific connection in the reported nodes.

issues.item: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled
issues.explanation: 'Fear Going Crazy' is not impossible in severe PTSD, but in this profile the dominant appraisal pattern is hopelessness/helplessness about bad things happening, while the threat items are generic startle/sleep symptoms rather than cognitive disorganization or intense internal alarm. This makes the 'going crazy' appraisal comparatively weakly integrated with the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, self-harm can occur clinically, but paired here with overeating and overworking as the only strategies, it stands out as a markedly different level and function of dysregulation. Without any corresponding memory intrusions, trigger-linked surges, or appraisals about guilt/shame/self-hatred, this specific item is hard to integrate with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
issues.explanation: Overworking is not impossible, but in this profile it fits weakly with the formulation because maladaptive strategies are strongly linked to threat and negative appraisals, while the rest of the profile emphasizes severe internal collapse and dyscontrol. Overworking suggests organized functional overcompensation, which sits awkwardly alongside self-harm and extreme hopeless/helpless appraisals as coequal primary strategies.

vignette:
Layla had always taken pride in her body’s strength. At thirty-six, she was one of the most respected crew members on her construction site, capable of hauling rebar and framing walls with an easy power that belied her frame. The heart attack, when it came six months ago, felt like a profound betrayal. It happened mid-shift, a sudden, crushing weight in her chest that buckled her knees and stole her breath. She remembers the grit of the concrete dust on her cheek, the panicked shouts of her colleagues, and the terrifying, helpless feeling of her own heart stuttering, failing. The weeks in the hospital were a blur of beeping machines and hushed conversations, but it was coming home that the real terror began.

Her body, once a source of confidence, had become a minefield. She lives in a state of constant, exhausting readiness, her muscles clenched as if bracing for a blow that never comes. The sudden roar of a generator on site or the clang of dropped steel will make her jump so violently she feels a jolt of pain in her neck. At night, sleep offers no escape. She lies awake for hours, fixated on the rhythm of her own pulse, certain that any flutter or skipped beat is the prelude to another attack. Her body feels perpetually on high alert, a tightly wound spring, and the physical exhaustion is immense. This relentless physical vigilance has become the lens through which she now sees the world, and herself. The constant tension and startling at every sound are not just symptoms to her; they are proof. They are evidence that her body is broken and that she is fundamentally unsafe. The experience has planted a deep, unshakeable belief that she is utterly helpless, that she has no ability to stop bad things from happening to her.

This pervasive sense of physical threat and the terrifying conclusions she draws from it have driven her to seek escape. The jumpiness and the feeling of being constantly on edge are unbearable, so she has learned to blunt them. At work, she throws herself into the most physically demanding tasks, pushing her body until pain and exhaustion are all she can feel, a strategy that keeps her mind too occupied to panic. When she gets home, the physical ache isn't enough to quiet the internal alarm. To achieve a deeper sense of quiet, she eats. She stands in front of the open fridge, consuming leftovers, bread, anything she can find, not for hunger but for the heavy, dulling effect it has on her senses. It's a way to numb the frantic energy inside her, to push down the fear until she feels almost nothing at all.

These strategies, born of desperation, have become a cage. The belief that she is going crazy, that her reactions are a sign of some permanent fracturing of her mind, fuels her need to numb herself with food and overwork. Yet, the aftermath only validates her worst fears. After a binge, the shame and physical discomfort that follow serve as fresh evidence of her loss of control, reinforcing the terrifying idea that she is irreparably damaged. The exhaustion from overworking on the job site makes her heart pound and her hands tremble, which she interprets not as fatigue but as the precursor to another cardiac event, deepening her conviction that she is helpless and has no future. The emotional numbing she works so hard to maintain has built a wall between her and her husband, whose worried glances she can no longer meet. His gentle questions about how she’s feeling are met with a shrug, leaving him on the outside and her more convinced than ever that a future of connection and happiness is impossible for her now. It was after he found her crying silently in the pantry last week, surrounded by empty food containers, that he told her he couldn't watch her disappear anymore. That, and the near-miss at work when her trembling hands almost caused a serious accident, is what finally brought her to therapy, terrified of the person she has become but even more terrified that there is no way back.
